headline: Layoffs stay rare. Jobless claims fall to 197,000.
summary: 197,000 Americans filed for unemployment benefits last week, the Labor Department said Thursday. That is the fewest since mid-July, and claims have stayed under 220,000 nearly all year, a historically low count. Employers are keeping the staff they have and hiring slowly: 80,000 jobs a month this year, against 9,700 a month in 2025.

cover_question.q: Did a lot of people lose their jobs?

cover_answer: No. Fewer than any week since July.
table_question: Would you rather have a safe job or lots of new ones to pick from?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Every week the government counts how many grown-ups lost their job and asked for help while they find a new one. Last week the count was the smallest since summer. Picture a packed stadium where a few people leave early: that's how few. Most grown-ups' jobs are steady right now.
5-7.why: A count of grown-ups asking for help is abstract. The stadium makes it a picture, and the last line is the one they keep. At this age they read your face before your words, so say it plainly.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old reads your face before your words, and "unemployment" on the radio sounds like a threat to the house. The script turns the count into a stadium where a few people leave early, one picture for the whole report, and ends on the line they keep: most jobs are steady. Expect "could you lose your job?" Say what is true.

8-12.script: When someone loses a job, they file a claim for unemployment checks. So the weekly count works like a smoke detector for layoffs: 197,000 last week, the fewest since mid-July. Bosses remember the hiring shortage after the pandemic, so they keep staff. Hiring is slow, though.
8-12.why: Lose a job, file a claim, the count moves. The smoke detector does the rest.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect, so the script runs a chain: lose a job, file a claim, the count goes up. The smoke detector turns a statistic into a gauge they trust, and the pandemic shortage gives bosses a reason a kid can follow. Expect "why is hiring slow if nobody's fired?" Keeping and adding staff are two decisions.

13-17.script: Is a job market where nobody gets fired but few get hired a good one? Claims hit 197,000 last week, the fewest since mid-July, but employers add 80,000 jobs a month, under half the 2023 pace. Second: bosses keep staff because the post-pandemic shortage scared them. Is fear a sound reason?
13-17.why: Low layoffs and slow hiring are both true. Let them pick which counts.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: layoffs are the lowest since July, and hiring runs at under half the 2023 pace. The script hands them both and asks which describes the job market. Kuhn says argument is practised, so let them argue the cheerful reading first. Expect "is it good news or not?" Good with a job. Harder without.

5-7.q: Did a lot of people lose their jobs?
5-7.a: No. Fewer than any week since July. Most grown-ups kept their jobs, and the ones who didn't get help while they look.

8-12.a: Money the government pays for a while after you lose a job.

8-12.q: Why do they count it every week?
8-12.a: It's an early warning. If layoffs climb, it shows here first.

13-17.q: Why is hiring slow if layoffs are so low?
13-17.a: Bosses keep who they have but add few. Rates and tariffs spooked them.
No. Under 220,000 is historically low, and it has sat there all year.
